title: Advanced Security: KMS, Secrets Manager, GuardDuty & Security Automation

scenes.narration: This chapter maps to two Professional exam domains: Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity, twenty six percent of the exam, and Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions, twenty five percent — because key policies, cross-account encryption, and automated threat response are fundamentally multi-account problems. Four ideas carry almost all of that weight. K M S — we'll just say KMS from here — encrypts through a mechanism called envelope encryption: a small data key does the actual encrypting, and the KMS key's only job is to encrypt that data key. Every KMS key also enforces a second, mandatory gate — its own key policy — sitting alongside I A M, not replaced by it. Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store both store secret values, but only one of them rotates credentials automatically. And GuardDuty turns from a dashboard into real automation only once a finding flows through EventBridge into a Lambda function that actually does something.

facts.label: The core mechanism

scenes.narration: Here's the trap nearly everyone falls into on their first KMS scenario, and it's a genuinely reasonable instinct: for almost every AWS resource, IAM is the only access-control gate that matters. Attach an allow-decrypt statement to a role, and for most services that's the whole story. Candidates carry that instinct straight into KMS and get baffled by an access-denied error despite a seemingly correct IAM policy. There's a second, related trap: seeing that Parameter Store can also store a secret string, and picking it purely because it's cheaper — when the scenario's actual requirement is whether the value needs to rotate automatically, not what it costs per month.

props.heading: "Full IAM access means full access" — and "cheaper always wins"
bullets: Attaching an Allow: kms:Decrypt statement to a role and assuming that alone settles it, the way it would for almost any other AWS resource.
Treating Parameter Store as a drop-in cheaper substitute for Secrets Manager, because it can also store a secret string.
Missing that rotation support, not price, is the actual requirement a database-credential scenario is testing.

scenes.narration: Walk through exactly why a permissive IAM policy alone doesn't decrypt anything. AWS evaluates the key's own resource policy — its key policy — and the caller's identity policy at the same time, for every single KMS call. Both allow it, you're through. The identity policy allows it, but the key policy never grants that principal permission and doesn't delegate to IAM at all — denied, and the key policy wins. The key policy allows it, but the identity policy never granted the action in the first place — still denied, because there's nothing to grant. And an explicit deny anywhere ends the conversation immediately, no matter what else says yes. This is why "I attached administrator access and decryption still fails" is a real, common incident, not a hypothetical.

props.heading: Every KMS call needs both gates to say yes

scenes.narration: Every "how does KMS encrypt my data" question resolves to one mechanism: envelope encryption. Your application never asks KMS to encrypt the actual payload — it asks for a data key, a small, random symmetric key, and KMS hands back two things: a plaintext copy for immediate local use, and that same key encrypted under your KMS key, safe to store. That plaintext data key encrypts your real data locally, at memory speed, with no size limit, and then gets discarded — it never touches disk. What you keep is the ciphertext plus the small encrypted data key. Decryption just reverses it: KMS decrypts that small key, one operation safely under its four-kilobyte limit, and your application uses it locally to decrypt everything else. This is the exact mechanism behind S three, E B S, and R D S encryption — you've been using envelope encryption this whole time without ever calling the APIs yourself.

props.heading: Envelope encryption, the way KMS actually does it
steps: Ask KMS for a data key — it returns a plaintext copy and an encrypted copy
The plaintext data key encrypts your actual data locally, no size limit
The plaintext data key is discarded immediately — only ciphertext and the encrypted key get stored
Decrypting reverses it: KMS unlocks the small data key, your app does the rest locally

scenes.narration: Lay them side by side and the deciding factor stops being price. Secrets Manager rotates credentials natively — for RDS, Redshift, and DocumentDB it can generate the rotation Lambda for you — and holds values up to around sixty four kilobytes. Parameter Store has no built-in rotation at all; you'd have to build that yourself with a Lambda and an EventBridge schedule, and its standard tier caps out at four kilobytes, eight on the advanced tier. So when a scenario says "credentials that must rotate automatically," Parameter Store's lower cost is irrelevant — it's disqualified by a missing capability, not a worse price.

rows.label: Max value size

scenes.narration: A handful of numbers resolve a surprising number of exam questions on their own. KMS's direct encrypt and decrypt calls only accept up to four kilobytes of plaintext per call — the entire reason envelope encryption exists for anything larger. Symmetric KMS keys support automatic annual rotation of their underlying material while keeping the same key ID, but asymmetric keys and any key with imported material can't use it. GuardDuty is regional and opt-in — turning it on in one Region detects exactly nothing in another; multi-region coverage means enabling it everywhere, or centralizing it through a delegated administrator account. And deleting a KMS key is deliberately hard to do by accident: AWS enforces a mandatory waiting period, configurable from seven to thirty days, specifically so an accidental scheduled deletion can still be canceled before every ciphertext that key ever protected becomes permanently unrecoverable.

props.heading: The numbers the exam turns into gotchas
bullets: KMS's direct Encrypt/Decrypt calls cap at 4 KB of plaintext — exactly why envelope encryption exists for anything bigger.
Symmetric KMS keys can auto-rotate their key material yearly, keeping the same key ID; imported or asymmetric material can't.
GuardDuty is regional and opt-in per Region — enabling it in one Region detects nothing in another.
Scheduled key deletion enforces a mandatory 7-to-30-day waiting period, specifically so it can still be canceled.

scenes.narration: Whenever a scenario says "respond automatically" or "without human intervention," it's describing this exact pipeline, not a dashboard someone checks. GuardDuty's threat-intelligence and anomaly models flag suspicious activity as a finding, and that finding publishes as a native EventBridge event. An EventBridge rule pattern-matches on the finding's severity and type, and when it matches, it invokes a Lambda function as its target — not a person. That Lambda is where "automatic" actually becomes concrete: it revokes the compromised session's credentials, or isolates the instance's security group, whatever the finding warrants. A Security Hub dashboard or an S N S notification gets you visibility, but visibility isn't remediation — without a wired Lambda action, "automated response" is really just "automated notification," and that's exactly the trap this pattern is built to catch.

props.heading: "Respond automatically" means this exact pipeline
steps: GuardDuty's threat-intel and anomaly models flag an event as a finding
The finding publishes in GuardDuty's native EventBridge event format
An EventBridge rule pattern-matches on severity and finding type
The matched rule invokes a remediation Lambda function as its target
The Lambda takes the actual action — revoking a session, isolating a security group

scenes.narration: Three commands map to the three moves this chapter is built around. Creating a KMS key with an explicit policy file is what actually decides who can use it — not the IAM permissions you attach afterward. Creating a secret in Secrets Manager encrypts it under that key by default. And calling rotate-secret with a ninety-day schedule and an AWS-generated RDS rotation Lambda is the managed capability Parameter Store simply doesn't have — you'd be hand-building all three of these steps yourself if you tried to replicate this with plain parameters.

scenes.narration: You'll never be asked to write these files from memory, but recognize the shape. key-policy dot json is the document that actually gates the key — a statement delegating to IAM within its own account, plus a separate statement naming any external account allowed to use it. secret-with-rotation is the two-call sequence you just saw: create the secret, then attach a rotation schedule. The EventBridge rule file is a plain pattern match on severity and finding type, and the Lambda is where the remediation actually happens. Being shown a snippet of one of these and asked "why does this still fail" is the actual skill being tested — not memorizing the syntax.

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. Northbeam Media runs a transcoding pipeline in one account that reads encrypted S three objects owned by a separate Data account. The transcoding role's IAM policy grants decrypt permission directly on the key's A R N — and every read still fails with access denied. Run it through the framework: the fix isn't more IAM permissions, because IAM was never the missing half. The Data account's key policy never named the Workloads account's role or account at all. Cross-account KMS access always requires the key's own policy to explicitly grant the external principal — the convenient "account root gets IAM delegation" shortcut only applies within the key's own account, and that's exactly the detail this scenario is testing.

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: a role has full K M S star permissions in its IAM policy, and a decrypt call still fails — what's actually going on? Second: leadership wants a class of high-confidence GuardDuty findings contained within minutes with absolutely no analyst review, across every account in the organization — which combination of services actually satisfies "no analyst review," and which ones only look like they do?

questions.prompt: A role has an IAM policy granting full kms:* permissions on a specific customer managed key. A call to kms:Decrypt using that key still fails. What's the most likely explanation?
options: IAM policies never apply to KMS keys — only key policies matter
The key's own resource policy doesn't grant that principal permission, or never delegates to IAM
KMS requires MFA on every Decrypt call regardless of policy
The plaintext data key has expired and must be regenerated

questions.prompt: Security leadership wants a defined class of high-confidence GuardDuty findings contained within minutes, with no analyst review, across every account in the organization. Which combination actually satisfies "no analyst review"?
options: A Security Hub dashboard the on-call engineer checks every few minutes
An SNS topic emailing the security team when a finding fires
An EventBridge rule matching the finding, invoking a Lambda that performs the remediation
A CloudWatch Logs entry reviewed during the weekly audit

scenes.narration: Here's why. KMS checks both gates on every single call — the key's own policy and the caller's identity policy each have to independently say yes. Full IAM permissions satisfy only one half of that; if the key policy never grants it or never delegates to IAM, the call still fails, no matter how permissive the identity side looks. And for the remediation question: only the EventBridge rule wired to a Lambda actually takes action without anyone in the loop. A dashboard, a notification, or a log entry all still depend on a human noticing and acting — they give you visibility, not the automatic response leadership actually asked for.

answers.prompt: A role has full kms:* in IAM, yet Decrypt still fails.
answers.correct: The key's own resource policy doesn't grant that principal permission, or never delegates to IAM.
answers.rationale: KMS enforces both gates on every call: the key's policy and the caller's identity policy must each independently allow the action. A permissive IAM policy alone can never succeed if the key policy doesn't also grant it — this is the one AWS resource where IAM is necessary but never sufficient by itself.

answers.prompt: Which architecture actually satisfies "no analyst review"?
answers.correct: An EventBridge rule matching the finding, invoking a Lambda that performs the remediation.
answers.rationale: Only the EventBridge-to-Lambda path takes an actual automated action. A dashboard, an SNS notification, or a log entry reviewed later all still require a human to notice and act — none of them satisfy "no analyst review," which is exactly the trap this pattern is built to test.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. KMS is a two-gate system: the key policy and the identity policy must both allow an action, which is unlike almost every other AWS resource you'll encounter. Envelope encryption is the real mechanism behind that encryption — a data key does the bulk work, and the KMS key only ever protects that one small data key. Secrets Manager's actual differentiator over Parameter Store is native, managed rotation, not its price. GuardDuty is regional and opt-in, and real multi-account visibility needs a delegated administrator, not forty separate logins. And whenever a scenario says "automatically," it means an EventBridge rule invoking a Lambda function — not a dashboard somebody has to remember to check.
